clinicalPearls: Allergic reactions span a spectrum from mild urticaria and pruritus to life-threatening anaphylaxis, and are among the commonest reactions to plasma-containing components.
Most reactions are due to recipient IgE or IgG antibodies reacting with soluble allergens in donor plasma.
Mild urticarial reactions without other features are the only category in which the transfusion may be paused, an antihistamine given, and cautiously restarted if symptoms settle.
Anaphylaxis presents with bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension and gastrointestinal symptoms, often within minutes and without fever.
Severe recurrent anaphylaxis should prompt testing for IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies, and for haptoglobin deficiency in susceptible populations.
Adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, with airway support, oxygen, fluids and adjunctive antihistamines and corticosteroids.
Washed cellular components and plasma-reduced or plasma-free products reduce recurrence in patients with severe or repeated allergic reactions.
Platelet additive solutions and washing lower the plasma load and the frequency of allergic reactions to platelet transfusions.
reference.pathophysiology: Allergic transfusion reactions are immediate hypersensitivity responses to soluble constituents of donor plasma. Recipient IgE (and sometimes IgG) antibodies recognise donor plasma proteins or other soluble allergens, cross-link on mast cells and basophils and trigger degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and other mediators. Localised mediator release produces urticaria and pruritus, whereas systemic release causes vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, bronchospasm and mucosal oedema culminating in anaphylaxis. A distinct severe mechanism occurs in individuals with congenital IgA deficiency who form anti-IgA antibodies and react to IgA in transfused plasma; an analogous process is described with anti-haptoglobin antibodies in haptoglobin-deficient individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Septic transfusion reaction from bacterial contamination
Unrelated drug reaction or latex allergy
additionalInvestigations: Serum tryptase timed from symptom onset to support anaphylaxis
Quantitative serum IgA with anti-IgA antibody testing after severe reactions
Direct antiglobulin test and haemolysis screen to exclude haemolysis
Observation of oxygenation and chest examination to exclude lung injury
Review of component type and plasma content
Consideration of haptoglobin deficiency testing in relevant populations
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness or tongue swelling indicating laryngeal oedema
Wheeze and respiratory distress from bronchospasm
Hypotension or collapse without fever suggesting anaphylaxis
Rapid progression of symptoms after only a small transfused volume
History of severe reactions with known or suspected IgA deficiency
reference.prognosis: Mild urticarial reactions are benign and often allow completion of the transfusion after treatment, whereas anaphylaxis is potentially fatal but usually responds well to prompt adrenaline and supportive care. Patients with anti-IgA-mediated anaphylaxis require lifelong precautions to prevent recurrence.
pitfalls: Restarting transfusion when features beyond simple urticaria are present.
Delaying adrenaline in favour of antihistamines when anaphylaxis is evolving.
Failing to investigate IgA deficiency after recurrent severe allergic reactions.
Overlooking the need for washed or plasma-reduced components in prevention.
Confusing an allergic reaction with lung injury or circulatory overload when respiratory symptoms dominate.
references: British Society for Haematology guidelines on the investigation and management of acute transfusion reactions
Mollison's Blood Transfusion in Clinical Medicine
management: Stop or pause the transfusion immediately and assess severity; isolated mild urticaria may allow cautious restart after an antihistamine
Treat anaphylaxis with intramuscular adrenaline as first line, alongside oxygen, airway support and intravenous fluids
Give adjunctive antihistamines and corticosteroids for anaphylaxis after adrenaline has been administered
Investigate severe or recurrent reactions with timed serum tryptase and test for IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies, and for haptoglobin deficiency where relevant
Prevent recurrence with washed cellular components, and provide IgA-deficient or washed components for IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA, using antihistamine premedication for recurrent urticaria
Report the reaction to the transfusion laboratory and haemovigilance system and document precautions for future transfusions
